Circles in Circles Sangaku

GeometryCirclesArea
Game: This is a drawing, not a game: four equal circles sit inside a big circle, and other circles fit in the spaces around them.
How to play: Drag X along the middle line, or focus it and use the arrow keys. Tick the boxes to show names, extra circles or colours, and press the buttons to jump to the special places.
Look for the math

Move X and the circles change size, but two of them always end up the same size. At one particular place a third circle joins them. Here is why, and how to find that place.

The four circles on the diameter

Let the big circle have radius r and centre O. Let x = OX, where X is the point where one small circle touches the diameter AB. A small circle of radius r1 has its centre r1 above the diameter and r − r1 from O. The Pythagorean theorem gives (r − r1)² = x² + r1², so r1 = (r² − x²) / 2r. Mirror that circle below AB and across O and you have all four.

The circle that touches all four

A circle centred at O and tangent to all four has radius r3. Its centre and a small circle's centre are r1 + r3 apart, so (r1 + r3)² = x² + r1², or r3² + 2r1r3 − x² = 0. The positive root is r3 = −r1 + √(r1² + x²) = x²/r. The two other circles of this size, at the top and bottom of the big circle, are drawn too.

The circle above the pair

Now take the circle touching the upper pair and the big circle inside. If its radius is r4, another right triangle gives (r − r1 − r4)² + x² = (r1 + r4)², which simplifies to r² + x² = 2r(r1 + r4). Put in r1 from above and you get r4 = x²/r. So r3 = r4 for every position of X — the test checks this at 3,603 positions on three board sizes.

The circle inside the lens

When the two upper circles overlap, a little circle fits in the lens between them. Its radius is r5 = r1 − x: the two centres are x apart inside a circle of radius r1. The lens is 2r1 − 2x wide. At x = r/3, r1 = 4r/9, so r3 = r4 = r5 = r/9. That is the 1837 sangaku from Aichi. The two buttons jump to both places that make it true.

Five circles in the regions

Turn on "Five-region circles" to see the drawing the article adds after the puzzle. The outer four of these circles always have radius r1, so together with the four original circles you get eight equal ones. When x = r√(3/5) the middle circle is also r/5, and all five are equal. The area each encloses is then π(r/5)². These region circles come from the applet's own drawing code; unlike the sangaku circles, the article does not claim they are tangent to their neighbours. The old applet picked a random starting X between r/4 and r/2 and showed no labels unless its page asked for them; here X starts at 0.4r and names are initially off.

Try pressing both r/3 buttons: the picture is a mirror image, but every radius is the same.

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)
